precedent.topic: Repair-context authorization, declaration, recency, and included evidence
quotes: | `get_repair_view` | owner, agent | one slot's repair read (A15 rule 6, K-12), not a list operation of A16 rule 6: `functions.read_slot`; the current contract version through `functions.read_contract_version` and its whole corpus; the current implementation through `functions.read_implementation`, with code, and its trial executions on the corpus — none, without an error, when the current contract version has no current activation; and through `store.page_records` the latest NodeExecutions of the slot's implementations — `page_size_default` unless the caller asks another size, at most `page_size_max` (A16 rule 6) — with a continuation token that also carries the implementation set of its first page; passed back, it pages only the NodeExecutions below that position for that set — an implementation added since has only newer executions, so nothing below is missed — and every other part is read again as of that request; the token is bound to its slot, so passed with another slot it is `invalid_request`, as the rule below the table says for every continuation token, and only the page size may change |

topics.topic: Authorization and privacy controls for direct agent-to-microservice access
questions: Is direct agent-to-service access part of the product, and if so, how is it authenticated and prevented from exposing files or personal data contrary to the kernel's disclosure rules?
What actor grants and controls this direct agent-to-microservice access, and how is it compatible with the statement that the owner is the only reader of personal data?
What external channel, credentials and authorization allow an agent to access a microservice directly, and how does this coexist with the stated kernel-mediated operation boundary?

quotes:
- **Owner** — the one human principal. Approves effects, accepts operation
  bindings, activates effectful flows, grants standing approvals, and is the only
  reader of personal data. Reaches the kernel through the agent channel with the owner's token.

An agent never receives a `personal_data` value: wherever the surface would
return one to an agent, it returns the value's digest and class instead. The
owner receives every value. This is one rule of the surface, not a per-agent
ceiling and not a redaction inside each operation.

Photo processing is not a kernel function: the agent processes a photo itself,
    outside the kernel, with its own access to the service that holds the photo —
    never through the kernel, which hands no caller a file — and the kernel moves
    the file between services.
judgement.divergence: One implementer gives the agent direct credentials and file-reading access to the service, while another denies direct access or requires an owner-mediated channel; the agent notices whether photo processing is possible and the owner notices whether the owner-only personal-data boundary is preserved.
judgement.why: The text relies on a direct agent-to-service trust boundary but does not name its authority, credential channel or relationship to the owner-only disclosure promise.

topics.topic: Cancellation semantics for functions and outbound operations already in flight
questions: What happens if cancellation arrives while an operation request is already in flight and its outcome is not yet known?
What happens if a function or HTTP operation is already executing when cancellation arrives, particularly when an effect request may already have left the kernel?
What happens if cancellation is requested while a function or HTTP operation is already executing, and how is its eventual result recorded?

judgement.why: The same cancellation question for executing functions and in-flight requests was already judged on unchanged texts.

precedent.topic: Cancellation semantics for already-running functions and in-flight requests
quotes: Requests are handled strictly one at a time, each to its end, run advancement included, before the next one is read (A18 rule 3).

Cancel, by the owner only, ends a run that has not ended as `cancelled`:
   nothing further is sent, every concluded record stays, undecided approvals can
   no longer be decided, and the spool is emptied.
precedent.why: The single-request execution model prevents cancellation from arriving concurrently with a running function or HTTP send; cancellation applies only after the active request ends.

quotes:
Only the owner decides, and only an approval that is `requested` in a run
   that has not ended; deciding any other is refused.

The request an approval covers is described, before sending, by: the method;

   wire, names lower-cased and in code-point order, each with its value, except
   that the credential header and `content-length` appear by name only — the
   length follows from the body described — and the `multipart/form-data`
   content type without its `boundary` parameter.

The body is described as the JSON body's bytes, or for
   `multipart/form-data` as the parts in order, each as its name, filename when
   present, media type and the SHA-256 of its content — the boundary, and the
   `content-length` it changes, are the kernel's framing of the parts the
   owner was shown, not a difference State 0 asks again for — so the boundary is not
   part of it: equal parts give equal descriptions. The `request_digest` is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of that
   description. The credential's value is never shown, so rotating it voids no
   approval; any other difference, whatever caused it, is a different request
   (owner decision 18).

the credential header's name, means the approval
   is no authority for this send: it stays `approved` and unused, void when the
   run ends, and the kernel proceeds as if it did not exist — under a grant
   when one applies, otherwise by asking anew as rule 2 says; or an active StandingGrant M25 for that
   node of the run's pinned flow version, when the node is not `destructive` and

quotes:
`contract_version_id` M03, `implementation_id` M05, `trial_case_id` M06,
   `flow_version_id` M13 and `value_id` M21 are computed by the kernel from the
   facts State 1 names for each, as the SHA-256 of their canonical JSON — RFC 8785
   (JCS), which fixes number formatting, string escaping and key order; a value
   JCS cannot represent (a non-finite number, a duplicate key) is refused where
   it enters, and no Unicode normalization is applied.

Submitting content whose computed identity already exists returns the existing
   record unchanged: its first author and time stay, nothing new is recorded for
   it, and it does not become "the one issued last". In particular an equal
   contract version does not become its slot's current contract version again.

topics.topic: Canonical digest construction and protection of low-entropy sensitive values
questions: Which canonical encoding and digest construction are used, and is the digest keyed or salted to prevent dictionary recovery of low-entropy personal data?
Which digest algorithm and canonical encoding are used for code, records and values, whether domains are separated, and whether personal-data digests are keyed to prevent offline guessing?

quotes: canonical_bytes: [BEHAVIOR] MUST parse json_text as one JSON value and emit its RFC 8785 (JCS) canonical form encoded as UTF-8: object members sorted by the UTF-16 code units of their names, numbers written in the ECMAScript shortest round-trip form (an integral double without a fraction or exponent, so a number written 1.0 becomes 1), strings escaped exactly as JCS prescribes, and no whitespace; it applies no Unicode normalization, so two texts that differ only in normalization give different bytes.

content_identity: [BEHAVIOR] For every content variant of IdentitySubject (contract_version, implementation, trial_case, flow_version, stored_value, corpus) MUST build one JSON object whose members are exactly the variant's fields keyed by field name, subject_kind included, with nested models as objects keyed by field name, tuples as arrays, enum members as their value text, None as null and JSON-text fields such as value_schema kept as JSON strings, take its canonical bytes with canonical_bytes and return the lowercase hexadecimal SHA-256 of those bytes.

content_identity: [BEHAVIOR] For the json_text variant MUST return the hexadecimal SHA-256 of the canonical bytes of json_text, and for the bytes variant the hexadecimal SHA-256 of content exactly as given, without any canonicalization; this is the digest of a file and of a value's bytes.
content_identity: [RETURN_SHAPE] Returns the 64-character lowercase hexadecimal SHA-256 digest as text.
judgement.why: The implementation notes specify unkeyed SHA-256, canonical JSON encoding, content-variant domain facts and the exact digest representation; no salt or key is used.

topics.topic: Installation ceilings, units, enforcement, and failures for resource and value-size bounds
questions: What units and maxima govern these bounds, whether contracts may choose arbitrary values, and which stated failure category represents exceeding memory, output or process limits?
What installation-level ceilings constrain author-declared resource bounds, and what refusal occurs when a contract requests more?
Where are maximum value and diagnostic sizes defined, whether bounds apply before or after encoding, and what observable failure occurs when a service returns too much data?

quotes:
Every global ceiling is one release constant `RELEASE_CEILING_<NAME>`, the
   name below in upper case, delivered to code as a data-provider constant
   (SPEC_STANDARD 15.3.1, 6.10: one exact entry is one scalar constant; owner,
   2026-10-03, raised by the pre-contract data closure). No
   request, flow, contract, manifest, configuration or environment variable raises
   one, and no module defines a second default. Release v1:

   | name | value |
   |---|---|
   | `wall_time_ms` | 30000 |
   | `memory_bytes` | 536870912 |
   | `output_bytes` | 67108864 |
   | `process_count` | 8 |
   | `sandbox_scratch_bytes_max` | 268435456 |
   | `implementation_code_bytes_max` | 1048576 |
   | `stored_value_bytes_max` | 1048576 |
   | `trial_fixture_bytes_max` | 67108864 |
   | `spool_file_bytes_max` | 134217728 |
   | `spool_run_bytes_max` | 536870912 |
   | `service_response_bytes_max` | 134217728 |
   | `transport_timeout_ms` | 60000 |
   | `surface_request_bytes_max` | 134217728 |
   | `bounded_text_bytes_max` | 16384 |
   | `failure_detail_bytes_max` | 4096 |
   | `page_size_default` | 50 |
   | `page_size_max` | 200 |

   The first four are the ceilings of the ResourceBounds M04 fields of the same
   name. Bytes are exact integers; times are integer milliseconds.

A bound above its ceiling is refused, never clamped. The refusal names the
   field and the ceiling. A bound omitted by the author is refused as well: the
   kernel supplies no default, because a default is a value nobody chose.

Outcomes are closed and checked in this order, the first that holds
   deciding: wall deadline passed — `timeout`; a limit hit (memory, process count,
   scratch, `output_bytes`) — `resource_exhausted`; a trap of rule 4 raised —
   `sandbox_violation`; the module failed to load, has no `run`, raised, or the
   process exited abnormally — `crashed`; the returned dict does not have exactly
   the output ports, or a value fails its port's schema, or a file output is not
   `bytes` — `contract_violation`; otherwise the execution succeeded. Output over
   the bound is a failure, never truncated.

Over a ceiling is always a refusal or a failure, never a truncation — for
   code, values, files, requests, responses and outputs. The exceptions are
   diagnostic texts, not values: `failure_detail`, cut to
   `failure_detail_bytes_max`, and a refusal's reason, cut to
   `bounded_text_bytes_max`, each at a UTF-8 character boundary.
judgement.why: Later rules enumerate every release ceiling and unit and define contract refusal, execution failure and diagnostic truncation behavior.

questions: What does the approve action return when the service is unreachable and the approved effect is not sent, as question 14 says the approval remains valid for resume?

quotes:
| nothing could be sent: name resolution, connection or TLS failed | `service_unreachable` | `service_unreachable`, attempt `not_sent` |
   | request may have been sent, no valid final response received (timeout, reset, EOF, a malformed status line or headers, only `1xx`) | `service_unreachable` | `outcome_unknown`, attempt `unknown` |

Reaching an operation element runs in this order: the pre-send checks of
   A09 rule 6 — a failure writes the element's next NodeExecution,
   `operation_failed`; then the authority of A10 rule 1, checked as it stands
   now — none for a `read`, the flow activation for a `draft-write` that is not
   a resend after `not_applied`, otherwise an approval or a grant; without it
   the element waits for approval, and after the approval this
   order starts again; then, for an operation other than `read`, one store call
   writes the EffectAttempt `in_flight`, naming the authority it uses — the
   approval, the grant, or for a `draft-write` send the flow activation
   (A10 rule 6);
   then the request is made; then one store call writes the outcome: the
   EffectAttempt's conclusion, the next NodeExecution, the values it produced,
   and the approval it used marked `used` — unless the attempt ended `not_sent`,
   which leaves it `approved` (M24). A crash between those two calls is the
   `in_flight` case of rule 4, whose recovery also marks that approval `used`.

On start, every EffectAttempt still `in_flight`, oldest first in store
   order and one store call per attempt, becomes `unknown`; when its
   attempt has no NodeExecution yet, the kernel writes it with status
   `outcome_unknown`, the binding as what it executed, the inputs the
   EffectAttempt names, no outputs, its start time taken from the EffectAttempt and its end
judgement.why: The service rules distinguish definitely unsent from possibly sent attempts and persist an in-flight record before sending so crash recovery produces an unknown outcome.

topics.topic: Pinned Python runtime, callable interface, encoding, and permitted standard-library boundary
questions: Which Python implementation and version are contracts admitted and later run against, and is that runtime identity pinned so deterministic admission and run replay survive upgrades?

Which standard-library modules are unavailable because they expose forbidden network, filesystem, clock, randomness, process or secret capabilities, and what failure is produced when code imports or reaches one?
Which Python implementation and version, module allowlist, source encoding and callable interface form the stable contract for implementations?

quotes:
The runtime is one Python interpreter with its standard library and nothing
   else, fixed by the kernel release (State 0 questions 4 and 17: photo processing
   is the agent's own work outside the kernel), started with a fixed
   hash seed (`PYTHONHASHSEED=0`) so that set and dict ordering repeats. Adding a
   library is a new kernel release.

An implementation is a Python module that defines a top-level function `run`
   taking one argument, a dict with one entry per input port, and returning a dict
   with exactly one entry per output port.

A release pins the exact versions of the kernel's Python dependencies and of
   the sandbox runtime (A03); the sandbox interpreter of release v1 is CPython
   3.12, whose `random` module gives A03 rule 4 its list. A vulnerable dependency is answered by a new
   release; a running kernel never updates one.

Before loading the module, the in-sandbox runner replaces every clock and
   randomness entry point of the standard library (`time`, `datetime` current-time
   functions, `os.urandom`, `random` seeding, `secrets`) with one that raises, and
   installs an audit hook that raises on socket, subprocess, `ctypes` and on
   opening any path outside the exchange directory and the read-only runtime.
judgement.why: Later function, installation and sandbox texts pin the interpreter, callable ABI and standard-library capability restrictions.

topics.topic: Prevention of personal-data leakage through control flow, diagnostics, timing, and trace metadata
questions: May an agent observe guard choices, map cardinality, failures, statuses, digests or other trace metadata derived from personal data, and if not, how are those observations classified or redacted?
How are exceptions, stdout, stderr, timing, resource usage and success/failure results from agent-written code prevented from disclosing personal data to the authoring agent?

quotes:
An agent never receives a `personal_data` value: wherever the surface would
   return one to an agent — run inputs and outputs, trial cases and executions,
   approval previews, trace records — it returns only the value's digest and class
   (K-14), and no `value_id`. The same holds for a `personal_data` file: an agent
   gets its digest and class, and not its size, media type or spool facts.

A
   `failure_detail` whose class is above `open` — the execution's class, raised
   for an operation's detail by the classes its binding declares for its outputs
   (A09 rule 7) — is returned to an agent only as its length and that class.

execute_function: [SECURITY_BOUNDARY] The sandboxed process's standard input, standard output and standard error MUST be connected to /dev/null, so nothing the code prints is read, kept, counted toward output_bytes or able to fill a pipe or the scratch area; code that writes without end is stopped only by its wall deadline and concludes timeout; the exception type and message reach the parent through the exchange channel, never through standard error (A03 rules 5 and 6).
judgement.why: Later models deliberately expose trace status, map identity, resources and times while masking personal payloads and classified failure text and discarding standard streams.

topics.topic: Repository inventory, access boundary, and linkage to admitted implementations
questions: Which repositories are required, who may access or modify them, and what kernel action, if any, records the relationship between repository content and admitted implementations?
Which repositories exist, who can read or write them, and whether repository access is through the kernel or an independent agent trust boundary?

quotes:
An implementation is immutable code for one contract version, identified
by the digest of the code together with its contract version.

A second agent with the same access continues the work from the kernel's
records, the platform manifest and the repositories alone.
judgement.divergence: One implementer treats named source repositories as required, independently accessible provenance linked to admitted implementations, while another relies only on implementation code stored in the kernel and treats unspecified repositories as optional; the second agent and owner notice whether repository access and provenance are needed to continue or audit the work.
judgement.why: The continuity promise depends on unnamed repositories without identifying their inventory, access boundary or relationship to admitted implementation records.

topics.topic: Schema language, canonicalization, and meaning of schema sameness
questions: Does 'same schema' mean identical canonical schema bytes or digest, structural equivalence, mutual assignability, or shared schema-version identity?
What schema language is used, how schemas are canonicalized, and whether “same” means byte identity, canonical structural equality or semantic equivalence?

judgement.why: The same schema language, canonicalization and equality question was already judged on unchanged texts.

precedent.topic: Schema language, supported types, canonicalization, and equality
quotes:
**Supported JSON Schema subset** (A02 rule 1, carried by States 1 and 2): a
   schema is a JSON object using only `type` (one of `null`, `boolean`,
   `integer`, `number`, `string`, `array`, `object`, as one string), `enum`
   (a non-empty array of distinct scalars), `const` (one scalar), `properties`
   and `required` (for `object`), `additionalProperties` (`true` or `false`
   only), `items` (one schema, for `array`), `minItems`, `maxItems`,
   `minLength`, `maxLength`, `minimum` and `maximum`.

"The same schema" means
   equal canonical JSON (State 1); two schemas that accept the same values but
   are written differently are different.
precedent.why: State 6 defines the schema language, while State 2 defines canonical equality.

topics.topic: Scope of the may-author permission across flows, bindings, functions, and trial cases
questions: Does the may-author flag govern flow composition and binding proposals as well as functions and trial cases, given that those Primary actions allow any agent?
Does the may-author right govern flow composition as well as function contracts, implementations and trial cases?

quotes: | author a function contract or implementation | agent with author right | the version with its identity — an existing one when the content is equal; the first contract of a new slot name creates the slot | invalid contract or code refused with the reason |
| add a trial case | agent with author right | the case — an existing one when the content is equal | a case whose values do not fit the contract's ports is refused |
| propose an operation binding | agent | proposed binding | manifest mismatch refused |

| compose and prove a flow | agent | the flow version and its proof result — proven, or the first failing edge or node (State 2, A05); the version is kept either way, and the first version of a new flow name creates the flow | an unproven version cannot be activated or run |
judgement.why: The primary-action table explicitly requires the author right for function contracts, implementations and trial cases but permits any agent to propose bindings and compose or prove flows.

topics.topic: Binding and pinned-run behavior after manifest drift or service-instance removal
questions: What observable node and run state results when a pinned binding no longer matches at invocation time: failed, pending, or refused without a run?
What happens to an already accepted binding and to a pinned run when the selected service instance is removed?

topics.topic: Contract-version succession and its effect on the active implementation
questions: What makes a later contract version the slot's current contract version, and what happens to the existing implementation activation when that occurs?

topics.topic: Deactivation when no safe rollback target exists
questions: How can the owner stop new runs of an active flow, or remove a function activation when no safe rollback implementation exists?

topics.topic: Declaration of accepted disclosure limits for function and flow inputs
questions: Where is the highest accepted disclosure class declared for a function input or a flow input, so the proof can check edges whose destination is not a binding input?

topics.topic: Definition and validation of typed-operation-to-HTTP request mapping
questions: Where and by whom is the deterministic mapping from typed inputs to HTTP method, URL, headers, body, target and response output defined and validated?

topics.topic: Deterministic ordering of proof failures across parallel branches
questions: What deterministic ordering defines the first failure in a graph with parallel branches?

topics.topic: Implementation, contract, corpus, and authorization selected by a trial execution
questions: Which contract version, implementation and set of cases does a try request select, and may an agent without the author right try unadmitted code?

topics.topic: Node and execution types eligible for capture as failed trial cases
questions: Is capture restricted to failed function-node executions, or can failures of operation, map or guard nodes also be captured?

topics.topic: Retention and response semantics when automatic implementation admission fails
questions: When valid code is stored but admission fails, is the implementation retained, and what single observable result does the submitting request return?

topics.topic: Retention policy for business values on edges and in traces
questions: May the kernel durably retain edge values that are themselves business facts, or must traces retain only digests while business values are discarded?

topics.topic: Revocation or disabling of an accepted binding
questions: How can the owner disable or revoke an accepted binding that was accepted mistakenly or is no longer trusted?

topics.topic: Run and node recovery behavior after process crash and restart
questions: What observable state results when the process crashes during a node execution or outbound operation, and which resting or active runs resume after restart?

topics.topic: Stable agent identity associated with configured tokens
questions: What stable agent identity is associated with a configured token, since tokens are described only as carrying a may-author flag?

topics.topic: Standing-grant validity across activation changes and reactivation
questions: Does a non-revoked grant remain usable by runs pinned to that version after another version becomes active, and does it become usable again if the old version is reactivated?

topics.topic: Whether agents may activate proven read-only flows
questions: Can an agent invoke activation for a proven read-only flow, as the Primary actions table and K-08 say, or is every activation operation owner-only as K-11 says?
